analysis.one_liner: Caps pay for temporary foreign farmworkers and loosens employer requirements in the H-2A guestworker program.
analysis.headline: A one-sponsor bill to cut required pay and protections for farm guestworkers never left a House subcommittee, drawing zero cosponsors and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The BARN Act would rewrite the H-2A visa program that brings temporary foreign workers to American farms. It would cap guestworker pay at 115% of the minimum wage — well below the higher wage growers currently must pay — and scrap the rule requiring employers to keep offering jobs to qualified U.S. applicants. It would also move the program from the Labor Department to the Agriculture Department, let employers pay a housing allowance instead of providing housing, and make it harder for farmworkers to get free legal help against their employers.
analysis.who_benefits: Agricultural employers who use H-2A visas. They would get a lower wage ceiling (115% of the minimum wage instead of the current, higher Adverse Effect Wage Rate), no obligation to hire qualified U.S. applicants during the first half of a guestworker's contract, visa applications deemed approved after 15 days of government silence, the option to pay a housing allowance instead of providing housing, and new limits on Legal Services Corporation lawyers visiting farms or taking workers' cases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Growers and farms using H-2A guestworkers

how_it_helps.text: Caps the required H-2A wage at 115% of the federal or state minimum wage, replacing the higher wage rate employers currently must pay guestworkers.
Eliminates the 50% rule, which required H-2A employers to hire any qualified U.S. applicants until half of a guestworker's contract had elapsed.

Requires the Agriculture Department to decide H-2A applications within 15 days, with applications automatically approved if the deadline is missed, and shortens the filing deadline from 45 to 30 days.

Lets employers in states where the governor certifies adequate housing pay a housing allowance at the local fair-market rent instead of providing housing directly, and frees them from reserving accommodations for workers.

Restricts Legal Services Corporation lawyers: they cannot assist an alien unless the worker is present in the U.S. and the parties first attempted mediation, must respect employer arbitration arrangements, and may not enter an employer's property without a pre-arranged appointment with a specific worker.

Moves program administration from the Department of Labor to the Department of Agriculture and expands the definition of covered agricultural work to include packing, processing, freezing, grading and similar handling of commodities.

analysis.who_pays: H-2A guestworkers and the U.S. farmworkers who compete for the same jobs. Guestworkers would face a lower wage floor, housing shifted from employer-provided bunks to a flat allowance they must spend on the open rental market, a two-month forced departure after two years, visa revocation after 60 days without work, and new barriers to the free legal aid they can use to enforce their contracts. U.S. farmworkers would lose the 50% rule, which gave them first claim on jobs for half of each guestworker's contract.

drawbacks.text: The wage cap would cut guestworker pay below the Adverse Effect Wage Rate that current law requires, directly lowering farmworker incomes.
Eliminating the 50% rule removes the guarantee that qualified U.S. applicants get first shot at jobs during the first half of every guestworker contract.

The legal-aid restrictions — mandatory mediation, deference to employer arbitration, and a ban on legal-aid staff entering a farm without an appointment with a named worker — would make it much harder for isolated, dependent guestworkers to challenge wage theft or unsafe conditions.

A housing allowance equal to average fair-market rent replaces employer-provided housing, leaving workers to find their own rentals, often in rural areas with little supply, while employers are released from reserving beds for them.

Moving the program from the Labor Department — whose mission is worker protection — to the Agriculture Department, which represents the farming industry, plus 15-day automatic approvals, would weaken oversight of employer compliance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow almost entirely in one direction: to growers, through lower wage obligations, faster and automatic visa approvals, lighter housing duties, and less exposure to worker lawsuits. The costs fall on the workers themselves — a lower wage floor, weaker housing guarantees, less time in the country, and stiffer practical barriers to free legal help. The bill does include real enforcement provisions, barring from the program workers who overstay or commit fraud and employers who knowingly hire overstayers or commit fraud, but those sit alongside a broad dismantling of the wage and recruitment protections that give farmworkers any leverage. Weighed honestly, this is an employer wish list with worker protections attached as a counterweight.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent down to its immigration subcommittee in April 2021, and no one ever moved it again before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Rick Allen introduced the BARN Act on February 15, 2021, with no cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day it was introduced.
On April 28, 2021, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Immigration and Citizenship, where it sat.
No hearing, markup, vote, or floor action ever followed, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farmworkers — both H-2A guestworkers and U.S. workers competing for the same jobs — kept the existing wage floor, the 50% hiring rule, employer-provided housing requirements, and access to legal aid, all of which the bill would have cut back. Growers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farmworkers kept existing wage and legal protections

for.name: Rep. Rick Allen
for.role: U.S. Representative, Georgia's 12th District; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and did not attract a single cosponsor in either chamber.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair and majority of the committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; after a subcommittee referral in April 2021, no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only record signals are a lone Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and a Democratic-run committee that never moved the bill.

industries.industry: Agricultural employers (farms and growers using H-2A visas)
industries.note: The bill would cut the wage growers must pay guestworkers to 115% of the minimum wage, end their duty to hire qualified U.S. applicants first, let them pay a housing allowance instead of providing housing, and shield them from legal-aid lawyers showing up unannounced. The savings come directly out of farmworker paychecks and protections.

industries.industry: Legal Services Corporation grantees (free legal aid for farmworkers)
industries.note: The bill would bar LSC-funded lawyers from assisting any alien unless the worker is present in the U.S. and mediation was attempted, require deference to employer arbitration outcomes, and ban legal-aid staff from farm property without an appointment with a specific worker. This narrows the main free legal channel farmworkers have to enforce their contracts.

The bill would strip the Labor Department of its authority over the H-2A program and hand it to the Agriculture Department, moving worker-protection administration to the department that serves the farming industry.
